claims.text: Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has porosity and low hardness of approximately 200 HV0.5.
The initial CoCrFeNiTi powder is compositionally heterogeneous and may contain Ti-rich regions that promote HCP formation.
High-energy mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering is a viable solid-state processing sequence for a high-entropy alloy.
Mechanical alloying followed by SPS will suppress porosity and achieve essentially full density in CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed processing will produce a fine-grained nanocrystalline solid solution.
The resulting CoCrFeNiTi structure will be dominated by FCC with a minor BCC phase.
The proposed processing will suppress formation of a brittle HCP phase in CoCrFeNiTi.
Severe plastic deformation during mechanical alloying homogenizes CoCrFeNiTi and suppresses HCP nucleation.
Rapid SPS achieves full density and preserves grain refinement without significant phase decomposition.
The mechanical-alloying treatment should be conducted for 40 hours at 250 RPM.
SPS should be conducted at 900–1100 °C with a heating rate above 100 °C/min and a dwell time of 5 minutes.
The processing should use an argon atmosphere.
The strain rate during sintering should remain below 10^-3 s^-1.
Ti content must remain below 15 at.% to avoid HCP dominance.
A cooling rate above 10 °C/min prevents HCP formation.
Oxygen introduced during mechanical alloying or sintering can cause an additional oxide phase and alter phase constitution.
The processed alloy will have hardness above 600 HV0.5.
The hardness increase will arise from a combination of grain refinement and solute strengthening.
The processed alloy will have porosity below 1%.

Nanoindentation at 10 mN with a 10-second dwell, combined with TEM grain-size measurement, can falsify grain-refinement strengthening if hardness does not increase significantly with grain refinement.

contradictions.description: The narrative says that the operating regime for dual-phase stability is not well-defined and that optimal temperature, heating rate, and strain rate require further research, while the other fields prescribe specific temperature, heating-rate, strain-rate, Ti-content, and cooling-rate limits without establishing that these maximize dual-phase stability.
